This verb means 'to cast out' or 'to expel.' In this verse, it indicates Jesus' promise to never reject those who come to Him. It underscores the welcoming nature of Christ and His willingness to receive all who approach Him in faith, thus reinforcing the idea that salvation is accessible to all.

37.epoque: In the time of Jesus, the Jewish people were awaiting a Messiah, and Jesus' teachings provoked diverse reactions, ranging from adherence to rejection. Religious and political tensions were palpable, and the understanding of salvation was often limited to the Israelites alone.
37.passage: This verse is situated in the chapter where Jesus presents Himself as the 'bread of life,' after performing the miracle of the multiplication of the loaves. He teaches that those who believe in Him will find eternal life, emphasizing the importance of faith and dependence on Him.
37.culture: In Jewish culture, the idea of coming to God was often linked to rites and sacrifices. Jesus, as the Messiah, overturns this notion by affirming that access to God is direct and personal, without intermediaries, which was revolutionary for His audience.
37.interpretation: This verse reveals the dynamic between divine initiative and human response. The Father draws those who believe, and Jesus promises to welcome them unconditionally. This highlights God's unconditional grace, which never rejects those who come to Him with a sincere heart.
37.commentaire: John 6:37 reminds us that salvation is a work of God, and that each of us is invited to come to Jesus, regardless of our past. As believers, we should rejoice in this promise and share this good news with those who feel distant, for Christ is always ready to welcome those who come to Him.

mots.sens: This term designates God in the highest sense, representing supreme authority and the source of all creation. In the context of John 6:38, it emphasizes the relationship between Jesus and the Father, highlighting that Jesus' will is aligned with God's. It also reveals the divine nature of Jesus, who acts as the agent of divine will on earth.

This word means 'will' and implies a divine desire or plan. In this verse, it is essential to understand that God's will is perfect and that Jesus, as the Son, is committed to fulfilling it. This highlights the idea that submission to divine will is an act of faith and obedience, essential for believers.

This verb means 'to descend' and evokes the idea of a deliberate and sacred action. In John 6:38, it emphasizes that Jesus comes from heaven with a specific purpose, that of doing God's will. This movement of descent also symbolizes the incarnation, where heaven meets earth, allowing humans to access divine will.

38.epoque: The passage is set in the first century, in a context where the Jews were awaiting a Messiah who would bring liberation and restoration. Jesus presents Himself as this Messiah, but with a spiritual mission different from what the people expected.
38.passage: John 6 deals with the miracle of the multiplication of the loaves and Jesus' teaching on the bread of life. This verse is part of a progressive revelation of His divine identity and mission, emphasizing the importance of submission to God's will.
38.culture: In Jewish culture, God's will was central, and prophets were often seen as instruments of that will. By affirming that He comes to fulfill this will, Jesus positions Himself as the true prophet and the Son of God.
38.interpretation: This verse reminds us that Jesus does not act according to His own desires, but is in perfect harmony with the Father's will. It teaches us the importance of seeking and following God's will in our own lives, submitting to His plans.
38.commentaire: John 6:38 calls us to a deep reflection on our own will in relation to God's. By imitating Jesus, we are invited to abandon our personal desires to embrace the divine mission. This encourages us to pray for knowledge and realization of God's will in all aspects of our lives, relying on His strength and wisdom.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to lose,' 'to destroy,' or 'to perish.' In the context of John 6:39, it underscores the divine promise of preservation and security for those who have been given to the Son by the Father. The theological significance of this word is immense, as it evokes God's faithfulness to keep His elect until the last day, reaffirming the doctrine of election and the eternal security of believers.

This verb means 'to raise up' or 'to resurrect.' It refers to the act of bringing to life, both physically and spiritually. In this verse, it highlights the Christian hope of the resurrection of the dead, a central promise of faith that assures believers that death is not the end, but a passage to eternal life in Christ.

This term means 'will' or 'desire.' It refers to divine will, highlighting that God's action is always in accordance with His perfect plan. In this verse, it reminds us that God's will is to preserve and resurrect those who believe in Him, thus emphasizing His love and sovereignty in salvation.

This word means 'gift' or 'offering.' It evokes the idea that believers are a gift from God to the Son, which underscores the intimate relationship between the Father, the Son, and the believers. It reminds us that our salvation is a gracious gift, and that we are precious in God's sight, reinforcing our identity in Christ.

39.epoque: The passage is set in the first century, in the context of Palestine under Roman occupation, where Jesus teaches and performs miracles, attracting the attention of crowds and religious authorities.
39.passage: John 6 deals with Jesus' discourse on the bread of life, where He explains that those who come to Him will never hunger or thirst. This verse emphasizes the guarantee of resurrection for those who believe in Him.
39.culture: In Jewish culture, resurrection was a central hope, linked to God's promises for His people. This context enriches the understanding of Jesus' promise to resurrect those who are given to Him.
39.interpretation: This verse underscores God's faithfulness to His promises. It assures believers that their salvation is secure and that they will be resurrected on the last day, which reinforces their hope and trust in Christ.
39.commentaire: John 6:39 reminds us that our salvation is entirely in God's hands, who will not lose any of those He has chosen. As believers, we can live with the assurance that our eternal life is guaranteed, and this should encourage us to share this good news with those who do not yet know Christ.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to see' in a physical sense, but also in a spiritual sense. In the context of John 6:40, it evokes a deep perception and understanding of the divine nature of the Son. This implies not only an external observation but an internal revelation that leads to faith. The theological scope is that seeing the Son is to recognize His divinity and His saving role.

This verb means 'to believe' or 'to have faith'. It goes beyond mere intellectual assent; it involves total trust and commitment to the person of Jesus Christ. In this verse, believing in Him is the means by which the believer accesses eternal life, highlighting the importance of faith in salvation. It also reveals the personal relationship that each believer is called to have with the Son.

This term means 'resurrection'. It evokes the idea of rising from the dead and is central to the Christian faith. In John 6:40, it assures believers that those who believe in Christ will be resurrected on the last day, thus affirming the Christian hope in eternal life. This underscores Christ's victory over death and the promise of eternal life for those who believe.

This word means 'life', but in a richer sense than mere physical existence. It refers to the eternal life that God gives to those who believe in Him, a life that is in communion with Him. In the context of John 6:40, this emphasizes that faith in Christ is the means to access this divine life, a life filled with meaning and hope.

40.epoque: The passage is set in the 1st century, in a Jewish context where messianic expectations were high and the resurrection of the dead was a topic of debate among believers.
40.passage: This verse is part of a discourse by Jesus on the bread of life, where He presents Himself as the Son of God. He explains that the will of the Father is that everyone who believes in Him should have eternal life.
40.culture: In Jewish culture, belief in the resurrection was present but often limited. Jesus expands this understanding by linking resurrection to faith in Him, which was revolutionary.
40.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that God's will is for all to have access to eternal life through faith in Jesus Christ. It establishes a direct link between seeing the Son and faith, affirming that resurrection is a promise for all who believe.
40.commentaire: John 6:40 reminds us that faith in Jesus is essential to receive eternal life. By seeing the Son and believing in Him, we are assured of the promise of resurrection. This calls us to deepen our relationship with Christ, to recognize Him as our Savior, and to live in the hope of the eternal life He offers.

mots.sens: The word 'ἄρτος' refers to bread, a staple food in Mediterranean culture. In the biblical context, it symbolizes not only physical nourishment but also the spiritual provision that God offers to His people. Jesus presents Himself as the 'bread of life', emphasizing that He is essential for eternal life, just as bread is essential for physical survival.

The term 'καταβάς' means 'descended', and it evokes the idea of a divine action where something from above comes down. This highlights the incarnation of Christ, who comes from heaven to bring life. Spiritually, it reminds us that Jesus is not just a teacher, but the Son of God who draws near to humanity to offer salvation.

The word 'Ἰουδαῖοι' refers to the Jews, a people chosen by God in the Old Testament. Their murmuring against Jesus reveals their resistance to accept His messianic identity. This highlights the conflict between religious tradition and divine revelation, and underscores the challenge that faith in Christ represents for those who cling to cultural and religious expectations.

41.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, during a time when religious and political tensions were high in Judea, under Roman occupation. The Jews were awaiting a Messiah who would liberate their nation, which influenced their perception of Jesus.
41.passage: In John 6, Jesus has just fed the crowds with bread and fish, a miracle that causes wonder. However, He then reveals Himself as the 'bread of life', provoking murmurs and misunderstandings among the Jews, who struggle to grasp His true identity.
41.culture: In Jewish culture, bread is a symbol of life and communion. The Jews had a strong tradition of dependence on God for their food, which makes their reaction to Jesus' declaration all the more significant, as they must reevaluate their understanding of divine provision.
41.interpretation: The murmuring of the Jews in response to Jesus' claim highlights the rejection of divine revelation by those who cling to their traditions. This underscores the need for an open faith and acceptance of the newness that Christ brings, even when it challenges our expectations.
41.commentaire: This verse reminds us that Jesus' coming as the bread of life is an invitation to nourish our souls through faith in Him. In the face of murmurs and doubts, we are called to recognize in Christ our source of eternal life. Let us accept this truth and share it with those who, like the Jews of the time, are still searching for meaning in their existence.

mots.sens: This word refers to Jesus, the Savior, whose name means 'Yahweh is salvation'. It is derived from the Hebrew 'Yehoshua'. In this verse, it is essential to recognize the divine identity of Jesus, which transcends His earthly origin. This highlights the duality of His nature, human and divine, and His central role in the plan of salvation.

This term means 'descended', coming from the verb 'καταβαίνω' (katabainō). It evokes the idea of movement downward, symbolizing the incarnation of Christ, who left heaven to come to earth. The theological significance here is immense, as it underscores Christ's humility and His divine initiative for the salvation of humanity.

The word 'πατήρ' means 'father'. In this context, it refers to Joseph, the earthly father of Jesus. This highlights the human perception of Jesus' origins and underscores the contrast between human understanding and the divine revelation of His identity. It reminds us that God's ways are often beyond our understanding.

This word means 'heaven'. In the context of this verse, it refers to the divine origin of Jesus. This emphasizes the fact that, although Jesus is perceived as an ordinary man, His true nature and authority come from heaven, which is fundamental to understanding His message and mission on earth.

42.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, during the earthly ministry of Jesus, in a Jewish context where messianic expectations were high.
42.passage: In John 6, Jesus teaches about the bread of life after multiplying the loaves and fishes. This verse illustrates the confusion of the Jews in response to His claim of having descended from heaven, highlighting their inability to see beyond His human appearance.
42.culture: At that time, identity and lineage were crucial in Jewish culture. People often judged others based on their family background, which explains their skepticism towards Jesus, whom they knew as Joseph's son.
42.interpretation: This verse reveals the tension between human perception and divine truth. Jesus' listeners cannot reconcile His earthly origin with His heavenly claims, which underscores their lack of faith and their need for spiritual revelation.
42.commentaire: This passage reminds us that our understanding of Jesus should not be limited to His humanity. Although He lived among us, He is the Son of God, come from heaven to offer us eternal life. We are called to move beyond our prejudices and embrace the revelation of who He truly is, in order to fully experience the reality of His salvation.

mots.sens: This term refers to a murmur, a complaint, or a grievance. It comes from the root that evokes the idea of whispering or discontent. In the context of this verse, it highlights the attitude of contestation and disagreement that can arise among those who hear Jesus' teaching. Spiritually, it reminds us of the importance of unity and faith in the face of divine teachings, rather than yielding to distrust.

This verb means 'to answer' or 'to reply.' It is often used in the New Testament to introduce significant responses or divine revelations. In this verse, Jesus' response to the murmurs of the people demonstrates his authority and desire to clarify the truth, thus emphasizing the importance of listening carefully to Christ's words without being swayed by doubts or murmurs.

43.epoque: This verse is set in the first century, during the earthly ministry of Jesus, a period marked by messianic expectations and religious tensions among various Jewish factions.
43.passage: John 6 deals with Jesus' discourse on the bread of life, where he proclaims his divinity and essential role for eternal life. This verse comes after Jesus performed miracles, but also after some began to doubt his teaching.
43.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, murmuring was often associated with rebellion, as shown in the story of the Israelites in the desert. Murmurs can also reflect disagreements on important theological issues, which were common in the context of rabbinical discussions.
43.interpretation: Jesus calls for no murmuring, emphasizing the importance of receiving his teachings with faith rather than succumbing to doubts. This reminds us that spiritual understanding requires an open heart and a willingness to accept divine truth, even when it seems difficult to grasp.
43.commentaire: This verse teaches us that murmurs and doubts can lead us away from the truth that Jesus offers us. As believers, we are called to listen carefully to his word and respond with faith, rather than yielding to the temptation of criticism. Let us cultivate an attitude of trust and humility in the face of Christ's teaching, so that we may grow spiritually and fully live out his truth.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to draw' and implies an action of force or persuasion. In the context of this verse, it highlights the divine initiative in the process of salvation, indicating that it is God the Father who draws the individual to Christ. This reinforces the idea that faith is not merely the result of a human choice, but of a divine intervention that prepares the heart to receive the message of the Gospel.

This verb means 'to raise up' and refers to the action of bringing back to life. In the context of John 6:44, it refers to Jesus' promise to raise up those whom the Father has given him on the last day. This underscores the Christian hope of resurrection and the certainty that those who believe in Christ will have eternal life.

This term means 'Father' and denotes the intimate relationship between God and believers. In this verse, it highlights the role of the Father in the plan of salvation, indicating that it is by his initiative that people come to Christ. This reinforces the idea of divine fatherhood and the unconditional love that God has for those he draws.

This verb means 'to come' and implies movement toward a place or a person. In this context, it emphasizes the importance of responding to God's call to come to Jesus. It evokes the idea that faith is an active response to the divine invitation, requiring a willingness to turn to Christ.

44.epoque: This verse is situated in the first century AD, at a time when Jesus was teaching in Galilee, confronted by crowds seeking signs and miracles.
44.passage: John 6 deals with Jesus' discourse on the bread of life, where he explains that he himself is the bread that comes down from heaven. This verse emphasizes the importance of divine initiative in the process of salvation.
44.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, the idea of being drawn by God was well established, as the people firmly believed in divine intervention in their spiritual lives and their relationship with God.
44.interpretation: This verse teaches that salvation is a work of God, who draws souls to Christ. It also emphasizes the certainty of resurrection for those who respond to this divine call, reinforcing Christian hope.
44.commentaire: John 6:44 reminds us that our coming to Christ is not the result of our own efforts, but a response to God's call. This encourages us to recognize God's grace in our salvation and to share this good news with those who do not yet know this divine invitation.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to teach' and is derived from the root 'didascalia,' which evokes the idea of transmitting knowledge or truths. In the context of John 6:45, it emphasizes the importance of divine teaching, which is essential for understanding God's will. The theological scope of this word underscores that God's teaching is fundamental to coming to Christ, as it reveals the spiritual truth necessary for faith.

This term means 'man' or 'human being,' and it is often used in the New Testament to refer to humanity as a whole. In this verse, it refers to those who are called to listen and respond to God's teaching. This underscores the universality of the divine call, indicating that all, without exception, are invited to come to Christ through the teaching received from the Father.

This word means 'the one who comes' and is related to the idea of movement toward a place or a person. In the context of John 6:45, it designates those who, after hearing God's teaching, move toward Christ. Theologically, this evokes the idea that faith is an active response to the divine call, where the individual spiritually moves toward the truth embodied in Jesus.

45.epoque: The passage is set in the first century, in a context where Jesus is teaching in Galilee, a period marked by messianic expectations and a search for spiritual truth among the Jewish people.
45.passage: In John 6, Jesus speaks of himself as the bread of life, and this verse emphasizes that God's teaching is essential for understanding who he is. It is a call to recognize the importance of divine teaching in the journey of faith.
45.culture: At that time, religious teaching was often based on the traditions of the ancestors, but Jesus emphasizes here that true teaching comes directly from God, challenging established norms.
45.interpretation: This verse reminds us that divine teaching is accessible to all and that spiritual understanding is a gift from God. Coming to Christ is a response to this teaching, which implies a personal relationship with the Father.
45.commentaire: John 6:45 invites us to seek God's teaching in our lives. As believers, we must be attentive to the Father's voice and his teaching, for it is through this that we come to Christ. This encourages us to nourish our faith through the word of God and to share this truth with those around us.

mots.sens: This word means 'father' and is often used to denote a relationship of authority and protection. In the biblical context, it refers to divine fatherhood, emphasizing the closeness and intimacy between God and His children. The theological implication here is that Jesus, as the Son, has a unique and direct knowledge of the Father, highlighting His authority and divinity.

This verb means 'to see' and implies a deep perception, beyond mere physical sight. In the spiritual context, it evokes understanding and revelation, indicating that seeing the Father is not just a matter of physical vision, but of spiritual revelation. This underscores the idea that Jesus is the mediator through whom we can know God.

This preposition means 'from' or 'out of' and indicates an origin or source. In this verse, it emphasizes that Jesus comes directly from God, thereby establishing His divine authority. This reinforces the idea that God's revelation occurs through the Son, who is both fully human and fully divine.

46.epoque: This verse is situated in the first century, at a time when Jesus was teaching in Galilee, confronting traditional Jewish religious ideas and messianic expectations.
46.passage: John 6 focuses on Jesus' discourse on the bread of life, where He reveals Himself as the spiritual source that satisfies the deep needs of humanity. This verse highlights the uniqueness of Jesus as the revealer of the Father.
46.culture: In Jewish culture, knowledge of God was often mediated through the Scriptures and the prophets. Jesus, by presenting Himself as one who has seen the Father, challenges these conventions and establishes a new understanding of the relationship with God.
46.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that knowledge of God is accessible only through Jesus, who is the sent Son. It reminds us that our understanding of God is limited without the revelation of Christ, and that it is through Him that we can truly know the Father.
46.commentaire: This passage invites us to recognize the importance of Jesus in our relationship with God. As believers, we must seek to understand the Father through the Son, for it is in Him that we find the fullness of divine revelation. This encourages us to deepen our relationship with Christ to better know and love the Father.

mots.sens: This term means 'believing' or 'having faith'. It implies not only an intellectual conviction but also a personal commitment to the truth of Jesus Christ. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes that faith in Christ is the means by which one accesses eternal life, revealing the depth of the relationship between the believer and the Savior.

This word means 'life', but it refers to a full and abundant existence, often in contrast to mere biological existence. In the biblical context, 'life' evokes a living communion with God, a spiritual reality that begins here and extends into eternity, thus highlighting the importance of faith in Christ to access this fullness.

This term means 'eternal' and denotes a duration that transcends time, often associated with divine life. In this verse, it indicates that the life Jesus offers is not only prolonged but is of a divine quality, allowing believers to participate in the very nature of God. This underscores the promise of an existence in communion with Him for eternity.

47.epoque: This verse was spoken in the context of Jesus' ministry in the first century, a time marked by messianic expectations and religious tensions between the Jews and the Roman authorities.
47.passage: John 6 addresses Jesus' discourse on the bread of life, where He reveals Himself as the source of spiritual life. This verse is central, as it summarizes Jesus' promise regarding faith and eternal life.
47.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, eternal life was a very important concept, often associated with resurrection and divine reward. Jesus redefines this notion by linking it to faith in Himself.
47.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the importance of faith in Jesus as the only means to access eternal life. It reminds us that this life is not merely a future promise, but a present reality for those who believe in Him.
47.commentaire: John 6:47 reminds us that faith in Jesus is essential for receiving eternal life. This encourages us to deepen our relationship with Him, recognizing that our salvation and spiritual life depend entirely on our trust in Christ. As believers, we are called to live this reality of eternal life now, bearing witness to God's love and grace around us.

mots.sens: The word 'ἄρτος' means 'bread' and refers not only to physical bread but also to the spiritual bread that sustains the soul. In the biblical context, bread is often associated with divine provision and communion with God. Jesus, by declaring Himself 'the bread of life', establishes a link between humanity's fundamental need for food and the spiritual necessity of being nourished by His presence and His word.

The term 'ζωῆς' means 'life' and refers to a full, abundant, and eternal existence. In the New Testament, this life is often related to the knowledge of God and communion with Christ. By presenting Himself as the 'bread of life', Jesus offers a life that transcends mere physical existence, promising a deep and nourishing relationship with Him.

48.epoque: This verse is spoken in a first-century Jewish context, where food traditions and symbols are deeply rooted in religious culture. The Jews had a strong understanding of divine provision through bread, notably through the remembrance of the manna in the desert.
48.passage: In John 6, Jesus teaches after multiplying the loaves and fishes, an act that illustrates His ability to provide for both physical and spiritual needs. This chapter addresses the nature of Jesus as the Messiah and the necessity of believing in Him to obtain eternal life.
48.culture: In Jewish culture, bread is a symbol of life and sustenance, and it is often used in rituals and celebrations. The idea of eating bread is intimately linked to communion and relationship with God, reinforcing the importance of Jesus' declaration.
48.interpretation: Jesus, as the 'bread of life', presents Himself as the essential source of spiritual life for those who believe in Him. This underscores the idea that spiritual satisfaction can only be found in Him, and not in material or temporary things.
48.commentaire: This verse reminds us that our deepest need is spiritual and that only Jesus can fulfill it. As the 'bread of life', He invites us to feed on His word and presence, to find fullness and eternal life. As believers, we must daily seek to be nourished by this bread that sustains us in our walk with God.

mots.sens: The word 'μαννα' refers to the miraculous food provided by God to the Israelites in the desert. Its etymology is uncertain, but it is often associated with the idea of divine provision. Spiritually, manna symbolizes humanity's dependence on God for sustenance, while highlighting the temporary nature of material goods, as those who consumed it eventually died.

The term 'θάνατος' means 'death' and evokes the separation of the soul and body. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the inevitable reality of physical death, even after receiving divine provision. Theologically, this reminds us that earthly life is fleeting and that true life is found in Christ, who offers eternal existence.

49.epoque: This verse is set in the context of Jesus' ministry in the 1st century, where he teaches and performs miracles in Israel, a people seeking signs and proof of his messianic identity.
49.passage: In John 6, Jesus refers to manna to establish a contrast between earthly food, which cannot give eternal life, and himself, who is the bread of life. This chapter addresses the question of faith and true spiritual sustenance.
49.culture: In Jewish culture, manna is a symbol of divine provision and the covenant between God and his people. It is often associated with the collective memory of the Exodus and God's faithfulness to Israel.
49.interpretation: The spiritual interpretation of this verse emphasizes that, just as manna nourished the Israelites, it could not give them eternal life. Jesus, as the bread of life, offers a personal relationship with God that transcends physical death.
49.commentaire: This verse reminds us that material goods, even those that are divine gifts, cannot satisfy our deepest spiritual need. As believers, we are called to seek not only earthly blessings but also communion with Christ, who gives us eternal life. Let us reflect on our dependence on him and how we nourish our souls each day.

mots.sens: The term 'artos' means 'bread' and generally refers to a staple food essential for survival. In the biblical context, it symbolizes not only physical nourishment but also the spiritual provision that God offers. As the 'bread that comes down from heaven,' it evokes divine revelation and communion with Christ, the true food that nourishes the soul and gives eternal life.

The verb 'katabainō' means 'to descend' and indicates a movement downward, often associated with a divine action. In this verse, it emphasizes God's initiative in sending his Son as a heavenly gift for humanity. This testifies to God's unconditional love and his desire to restore the relationship with man through Christ.

The word 'thanatos' means 'death' and can refer to both physical death and spiritual separation from God. In this verse, it highlights the promise of eternal life for those who accept Christ as their bread of life. This underscores the importance of faith in Jesus to escape spiritual death and access the fullness of life in Him.

50.epoque: This verse is situated in the first century, at a time when Jesus was preaching in Israel, a country under Roman rule, where messianic expectations were high among the Jewish people.
50.passage: John 6 discusses the miracle of the multiplication of the loaves and the subsequent conversation between Jesus and the crowd, where He reveals himself as the bread of life. This chapter emphasizes the necessity of authentic faith in Him to receive eternal life.
50.culture: In Jewish culture, bread is a symbol of sustenance and divine blessing, often associated with the manna that God provided to the Israelites in the desert. This reference to spiritual food resonates deeply with Jesus' audience.
50.interpretation: This verse reveals that Jesus is the heavenly bread, essential for spiritual life. By partaking of him, that is, by receiving him through faith, believers escape spiritual death and access eternal life, a fundamental promise of Christianity.
50.commentaire: This passage reminds us that our dependence on Christ is as vital as our need for daily bread. By accepting Jesus as our bread of life, we experience a spiritual transformation that frees us from death and offers us eternal communion with God. He calls us to nourish our souls through his word and presence, so that we may live fully in the abundance of life he offers.

mots.sens: The word 'ἄρτος' means 'bread' and refers not only to physical food but also as a symbol of spiritual sustenance. In the biblical context, bread is often associated with divine providence and communion with God. Here, Jesus presents himself as the living bread, indicating that his presence and sacrifice are essential for the eternal life of believers.

The term 'ζωὴ' means 'life' and refers to a full and abundant existence, both physically and spiritually. In the New Testament, it is often used to describe the eternal life that Jesus offers to those who believe in him. This word emphasizes the idea that true life does not come merely from biological existence, but from a living relationship with Christ.

The word 'σάρξ' means 'flesh' and refers to human nature, often in opposition to the spirit. In this verse, it symbolizes the sacrifice of Jesus, who gave his flesh for the salvation of the world. This term underscores the incarnation of Christ and the importance of his physical sacrifice for the redemption of humanity.

51.epoque: This verse is set in the first century, at a time when Judaism was in full swing and messianic expectations were high. Jesus, as a rabbi and prophet, challenged established religious norms while revealing his divine nature.
51.passage: John 6 focuses on Jesus' discourse on the bread of life, following the miracle of the multiplication of the loaves. This chapter shows how Jesus uses this event to teach profound truths about his mission and identity.
51.culture: In Jewish culture, bread is a staple food, symbolizing life and communion. The notion of eating the flesh of Jesus was shocking to the listeners, as it challenged sacred and traditional concepts related to purity and sacrifice.
51.interpretation: Jesus presents himself as the living bread, emphasizing that his flesh, given for the world, is essential for eternal life. This reveals that faith in him and acceptance of his sacrifice are necessary to receive spiritual life. This passage invites believers to a deep communion with Christ.
51.commentaire: This verse reminds us that Jesus is our source of spiritual life. By accepting his sacrifice, we enter into a living relationship with him, which transforms us and gives us the hope of eternal life. He calls us to nourish our souls with his word and presence, so that we may live fully according to his will.

mots.sens: The word 'sarx' refers to flesh, the physical organ of the human being, but it also has spiritual connotations. In the biblical context, it can symbolize human nature, often in opposition to the spirit. Here, it emphasizes the mystery of communion with Christ, who offers himself as spiritual food, inviting believers into a deep and intimate relationship with him.

The verb 'didomi' means 'to give' and implies an act of generosity or sacrifice. In the context of this verse, it highlights the idea that Jesus gives himself entirely to believers. This evokes the notion of Christ's sacrificial love, who gives himself for the life of the world, and invites reflection on the depth of his commitment to humanity.

52.epoque: In the 1st century, Jewish society was marked by messianic expectations and a strong religious tradition. The Jews were in search of a Messiah who would liberate them, but Jesus' message often clashed with their established expectations.
52.passage: This passage is part of Jesus' discourse on the bread of life, where he reveals himself as the source of eternal life. It provokes reactions of confusion and rejection among the Jews, who struggle to understand the meaning of his words.
52.culture: In Jewish culture, the consumption of flesh was governed by strict dietary laws, and the idea of eating the flesh of a man was inconceivable. This reflects a tension between divine revelation and human traditions.
52.interpretation: This verse highlights the difficulty of accepting the spiritual truth that Jesus presents. It invites reflection on how we perceive the work of Christ and our relationship with him as the source of spiritual life.
52.commentaire: This passage reminds us that faith in Christ requires an acceptance of his sacrifice and his presence in our lives. By offering us his flesh, Jesus calls us to a deep communion with him that transcends the limits of our human understanding. We are invited to move beyond our doubts and embrace the truth of his promise of eternal life.

mots.sens: The word 'sarx' refers to flesh, the physical body of man. In the biblical context, it evokes not only the material dimension of the human being but also connotations of weakness and sin. Spiritually, eating the flesh of the Son of Man symbolizes the appropriation of Christ's life, an intimate communion with Him that is essential for eternal life.

The term 'haima' means blood, often associated with life in Jewish culture. In Christian theology, the blood of Jesus is the symbol of sacrifice and atonement for sins. By drinking his blood, believers engage in a relationship of grace and redemption, affirming that true life can only be found in Christ.

53.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, at a time when Jesus was preaching in Galilee, confronting the religious and cultural expectations of his time.
53.passage: In John 6, Jesus teaches about the bread of life after miraculously feeding a crowd. This chapter emphasizes the necessity of believing in Him to have eternal life.
53.culture: In Jewish culture, sharing bread and wine was an act of communion and intimacy. The metaphors of flesh and blood were radical and provoked strong reactions among the listeners.
53.interpretation: Jesus' invitation to eat his flesh and drink his blood is a powerful metaphor illustrating the necessity of a living faith and spiritual communion with Him. It emphasizes that eternal life can only be acquired through a personal relationship with Christ.
53.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the importance of communion with Christ in our spiritual life. By accepting Jesus' sacrifice, we receive eternal life. This calls us to nourish our souls through the Word of God and to live in constant relationship with our Savior.

mots.sens: The word 'sarx' refers to flesh, representing both the physical body and human nature in its weakness. In the context of John 6:54, it symbolizes the incarnation of Christ, emphasizing the importance of his suffering and sacrifice. Spiritually, eating the flesh of Christ evokes the acceptance of his sacrifice for the forgiveness of sins and access to eternal life.

The term 'haima' means blood, often associated with life and sacrifice in Jewish tradition. In this verse, it refers to the blood shed by Jesus during his crucifixion, which is the means by which believers are cleansed from their sins. Theologically, drinking the blood of Christ is a powerful metaphor for communion and participation in his divine life.

The word 'zoe' means life, but in a deeper sense than mere physical existence. It refers to eternal life, a quality of life that only Christ can give, which begins here and extends into eternity. This life is intrinsically linked to the relationship with Jesus, the Bread of Life.

The term 'anastasis' means resurrection, evoking the raising of the dead at the end of times. In this verse, it underscores Jesus' promise to resurrect those who believe in him, thus affirming his power over death. This brings profound hope to believers, assuring them of eternal life with Christ.

54.epoque: The historical context of this passage is situated in the 1st century, in a Jewish environment under Roman domination, where messianic expectations were high. Jesus' teachings challenged established religious traditions and invited a new understanding of faith.
54.passage: In John 6, Jesus teaches about the Bread of Life after multiplying the loaves and fishes. This discourse provokes varied reactions among his listeners, some being troubled by his words about flesh and blood.
54.culture: Jewish culture valued sacrifice and blood as essential elements for the atonement of sins. References to the flesh and blood of Jesus resonate with the sacrificial practices of the temple, but Jesus' teachings introduce a new spiritual dimension.
54.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the importance of spiritual communion with Christ, where eating his flesh and drinking his blood symbolize the acceptance of his sacrifice and the commitment to live according to his teachings. It also reveals the promise of eternal life for those who believe in him.
54.commentaire: John 6:54 reminds us that faith in Christ is not merely an intellectual belief but a deep communion with him. By participating in his sacrifice, we receive eternal life and the assurance of resurrection. This passage calls us to spiritually nourish ourselves with the Word of God and to live in communion with our Savior.

mots.sens: The word 'sarx' refers to flesh in the physical sense, but also to human nature in its weakness and mortality. In this verse, it evokes the reality of Christ's incarnation, emphasizing that His flesh is an essential spiritual nourishment for believers. This relates to the notion that, through His flesh, Jesus offers eternal life, thus connecting the physical body to spiritual salvation.

The term 'haima' means blood, a symbol of life and sacrifice in Jewish culture. In the Christian context, the blood of Jesus represents the means by which sins are atoned. This verse highlights the importance of Christ's sacrifice, which, through His blood, establishes a new covenant between God and humanity, thus offering complete redemption.

55.epoque: In the first century, Palestine was under Roman rule, and Judaism was in full swing, with strong messianic expectations among the people. Jesus presented Himself as the Messiah, challenging established religious norms and announcing a new way to God.
55.passage: John 6 presents Jesus' discourse on the bread of life, where He reveals Himself as the source of eternal life. In this chapter, Jesus teaches that true food and true drink come from Himself, which shocks and challenges the listeners.
55.culture: In Jewish culture, sharing bread and wine was a sacred act, symbolizing communion and covenant. Jesus uses these symbols to illustrate the depth of the relationship He establishes with His disciples through His sacrifice.
55.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the necessity of an intimate communion with Christ to receive eternal life. The flesh and blood of Jesus are not merely physical elements but also represent the spiritual commitment of believers to feed on His truth and sacrifice.
55.commentaire: John 6:55 reminds us that our spiritual life depends on our relationship with Jesus, who gives Himself to us as food and drink. By accepting His sacrifice, we are nourished and renewed, enabling us to live fully for Him. This verse invites us to reflect on our dependence on Christ and to seek daily this communion that strengthens us in our faith.

mots.sens: The word 'sarx' refers to flesh, representing human nature, often in opposition to the spirit. In the context of John 6:56, it evokes the incarnation of Christ, emphasizing that His flesh is essential for communion with Him. This relates to the notion of sacrifice and life given, having major theological implications in understanding the Eucharist and the intimate relationship between the believer and Christ.

The term 'haima' means blood, a symbol of life and sacrifice in Jewish tradition. In this verse, the blood of Christ evokes the new covenant, sealed by His sacrifice on the cross. Spiritually, this reinforces the idea that the believer is purified and reconciled with God through the blood of Christ, a central truth of the Christian faith.

The verb 'menō' means to remain or stay, indicating a relationship of closeness and continuity. In the context of John 6:56, it emphasizes the idea that those who partake of the flesh and blood of Christ enter into a deep and lasting communion with Him. This implies a life of active faith, where the believer finds their source and strength in Christ.

The preposition 'en' expresses a notion of interiority or connection. In this verse, it indicates that communion with Christ is a spiritual reality where the believer is in Him and vice versa. This underscores the intimacy of the relationship between the believer and Christ, essential for an authentic Christian life.

56.epoque: This passage was written in the first century, at a time when Judaism and Christianity were evolving, with tensions between religious traditions and new beliefs in Christ.
56.passage: John 6 deals with the discourse on the bread of life, where Jesus reveals His divine nature and His role as the source of spiritual life. This verse is set in a context where Jesus teaches about the importance of His flesh and blood for eternal life.
56.culture: In Jewish culture, sharing a meal was an act of communion and connection. The mention of eating and drinking the flesh and blood of Jesus evokes a deep and sacred relationship, in contrast to the ritual practices of the time.
56.interpretation: This verse emphasizes the importance of communion with Christ for the spiritual life of the believer. Eating His flesh and drinking His blood symbolize the acceptance of His sacrifice and the entrance into a living and dynamic relationship with Him. This reminds us that our Christian life is nourished by our union with Christ.
56.commentaire: John 6:56 calls us to a deep communion with Jesus, who is our source of life. By participating in His sacrifice, we are invited to remain in Him, which transforms our existence. This verse encourages us to seek this intimacy with Christ every day, through prayer, meditation on the Word, and participation in communion.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to live', 'to have life'. It expresses not only physical existence but also a rich and abundant spiritual life. In the context of John 6:57, it underscores the vital relationship between Jesus and those who believe in Him, indicating that spiritual life is nourished by communion with Christ, just as Jesus lives by the Father.

This verb means 'to eat' in the literal sense, but it also carries a connotation of intimate consumption and participation. In this verse, it evokes the idea of appropriating Jesus, engaging in a deep relationship with Him, emphasizing that spiritual life is nourished by this communion. This reinforces the importance of active faith and the acceptance of Christ in the believer's life.

This word means 'father' and is central to understanding the relationship between Jesus and God. It evokes authority, protection, and the source of life. In the context of John 6:57, it emphasizes that the life of Jesus is directly linked to that of the Father, establishing a model for believers: to live by and for Christ, just as Jesus lives by the Father.

This term means 'life', but it refers to a spiritual and eternal life. In the New Testament, it is often used to describe the life that Christ offers to believers. In John 6:57, it is essential to understand that this life is accessible through faith in Jesus, who Himself is the source of this eternal life.

57.epoque: In the first century, Palestine was under Roman occupation, and Judaism was evolving, with strong messianic expectations among the people. Jesus' teachings took place in a context of religious and political tensions.
57.passage: John 6 deals with the discourse on the bread of life, where Jesus reveals Himself as the true bread that comes down from heaven. This chapter is crucial as it establishes the necessity of believing in Him to have eternal life.
57.culture: In Jewish culture, meals and sharing food are powerful symbols of communion and intimacy. Eating together was an act of relationship and sharing, reinforcing the idea that faith in Christ involves a personal and deep relationship.
57.interpretation: John 6:57 illustrates the spiritual dependence of believers on Christ, just as Jesus depends on the Father. This emphasizes the idea that eternal life is a reality lived daily through faith and communion with Christ.
57.commentaire: This verse reminds us that our spiritual life depends entirely on our relationship with Jesus. By 'eating' Him, we accept His life within us, nourishing ourselves with His word and presence. This calls us to an active faith, where we seek each day to live in communion with Him, in order to receive the life He promises.

mots.sens: The word 'ἄρτος' means 'bread' and refers not only to a physical food but also to a symbol of spiritual life. In the context of John 6:58, it evokes the heavenly bread, which is Christ himself, in contrast to the earthly manna that nourished the ancestors but did not provide eternal life. This term emphasizes the idea that Jesus is the true food that grants eternal life, a central notion in Christian theology.

The term 'ζάω' means 'to live' and implies a full and abundant existence, both physically and spiritually. In this verse, it is used to describe the promise of eternal life granted to those who eat the bread that comes down from heaven, that is, Jesus. This underscores the eschatological dimension of the Christian faith, where communion with Christ ensures a life that transcends physical death.

The word 'θάνατος' means 'death' and evokes not only the cessation of physical life but also spiritual separation from God. In the context of John 6:58, it is used to contrast the death of the ancestors who ate the manna with the promise of eternal life offered by Christ. This highlights Jesus' victory over death and the hope of resurrection for those who believe in him.

58.epoque: This passage was written in the first century, at a time when the Jews were seeking their religious and spiritual identity, in a context of Roman domination and messianic expectations.
58.passage: John 6 deals with Jesus' discourse on the bread of life, where he reveals himself as the bread that comes down from heaven, in response to the spiritual needs of the crowds who had followed him after the miracle of the multiplication of the loaves.
58.culture: In Jewish culture, bread is a staple food, symbolizing sustenance and God's blessing. The manna, which nourished the Israelites in the desert, is a central element of their collective memory and their relationship with God.
58.interpretation: This verse emphasizes that Jesus is the true bread that provides eternal life, in contrast to earthly foods that cannot save. It invites believers to spiritually feed on him to live fully and eternally.
58.commentaire: John 6:58 reminds us that our true source of life does not lie in material goods, but in Christ. By accepting Jesus as the bread of life, we enter into a transformative relationship that assures us of eternal life. This verse calls us to a daily communion with him, nourishing our souls and strengthening our faith.

mots.sens: The term 'συναγωγή' refers to an assembly or a gathering place for worship and teaching. In the Jewish context, the synagogue was not only a place of prayer but also a center for teaching the Law. Spiritually, this underscores the importance of communal teaching and fellowship in faith, where Jesus positions himself as the divine authority who reveals the truth.

The verb 'διδάσκω' means to teach or instruct. This word implies a transmission of knowledge, often with a connotation of authority and wisdom. In this verse, it highlights Jesus' role as Master and Teacher, bringing a divine revelation that transcends mere human knowledge and calls for a response of faith.

Capernaum is a city located by the Sea of Galilee, often mentioned in the Gospels as the site of many of Jesus' miracles. As a center of his ministry, it represents a spiritual crossroads where God's revelation is powerfully manifested. This place thus becomes a witness to Jesus' teachings and the impact of his saving mission.

59.epoque: In the first century, Palestine was under Roman occupation, and Judaism was experiencing significant religious and social fervor, with growing messianic expectations among the Jewish people.
59.passage: This verse is part of a larger discourse where Jesus teaches about the 'bread of life', revealing profound truths about his divine nature and salvific role. It takes place in the synagogue of Capernaum, a key location in his ministry.
59.culture: The synagogue was a central place in Jewish life, where people gathered not only to pray but also to study the Scriptures and discuss matters of faith. This shows the importance of teaching in Jewish culture.
59.interpretation: Jesus teaches in a sacred place, affirming his divine authority and role as teacher. This passage underscores the necessity of listening to and understanding his words, which are essential for the spiritual life of believers.
59.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the importance of Jesus' teaching in our daily lives. As believers, we are called to seek his word and gather together to learn, while recognizing that his truth is the foundation of our faith and communion with God. Let us commit to listening to and applying his teachings in our lives.

mots.sens: The term 'logos' refers to the word, discourse, or principle. In the context of John 6:60, it refers to Jesus' teaching, which is both revealing and provocative. This word emphasizes the idea that the word of God has a transformative power, but it can also be difficult to accept for those who are not ready to receive its truth.

This word means 'hard' or 'difficult'. In this verse, it expresses the reaction of the disciples to Jesus' teaching, which exceeds their understanding. The hardness of this word reveals the depth of commitment required to follow Christ and the challenges it entails for believers in their daily lives.

The verb 'akouo' means 'to listen' or 'to hear'. Here, it underscores the importance of attentively listening to the word of Jesus, which requires not only physical hearing but also a spiritual disposition. This highlights the fact that listening to divine truth can elicit varied reactions depending on the disposition of the heart.

60.epoque: This passage takes place in the first century, in a context where Jesus was teaching in Galilee, a region marked by religious tensions and messianic expectations among the Jewish people.
60.passage: John 6 deals with Jesus' discourse on the bread of life, where he reveals his divine identity and the necessity of believing in him to have eternal life. This verse illustrates the difficulty some disciples experience in accepting this radical teaching.
60.culture: At that time, the Jews had specific expectations regarding the Messiah and the nature of his kingdom. The idea that the Messiah might demand total commitment and inner transformation was bewildering for many.
60.interpretation: The disciples recognize that Jesus' word is difficult to accept, reflecting the human struggle in facing divine truth. This reminds us that following Christ often requires overcoming our own prejudices and limited understanding.
60.commentaire: This verse invites us to reflect on our own disposition to listen to the word of God. In the face of teachings that may seem hard or perplexing, we are called to seek understanding and faith, knowing that God's truth can profoundly transform us. Let us be ready to embrace the challenges that faith in Christ may pose in our daily lives.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to cause to stumble' or 'to scandalize.' It is derived from 'skandalon,' which refers to a trap or a stumbling block. In this context, it evokes the reaction of the disciples to Jesus' teaching, which prompts them to question their faith. This underscores the importance of faith and understanding in the relationship with Christ, as what scandalizes can also be an opportunity for spiritual growth.

This term means 'disciple' or 'student.' It refers to those who follow a teacher to learn from him. In the context of this verse, it highlights the learning relationship between Jesus and his disciples, emphasizing that even those who are close to him may face difficulties in understanding. This reminds us that the path of faith is often fraught with challenges, but it is essential to persevere in learning.

This word means 'word' or 'speech.' It is often used to refer to divine teaching or revelation. In this passage, it refers to the words of Jesus that may seem harsh or difficult to accept. This highlights the power and authority of God's word, which can provoke varied reactions among those who hear it, but is always intended to lead to the truth.

61.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, in the context of Palestine under Roman occupation, where Judaism was experiencing significant religious and political fervor.
61.passage: John 6 deals with the miracle of the multiplication of the loaves and Jesus' teachings on the bread of life. This verse comes after Jesus has shared profound truths about his identity and mission, provoking murmurs among his disciples.
61.culture: In Jewish culture, respect for teachings and traditions was paramount. The words of Jesus challenged established norms, which could be perceived as an affront or provocation.
61.interpretation: Jesus, aware of the murmurs, poses a question that invites reflection on faith and spiritual understanding. This moment underscores that the truth of the Gospel can sometimes be difficult to accept, but it is essential for true communion with him.
61.commentaire: This verse reminds us that our faith can be tested by difficult teachings. It is crucial not to let the scandal of Jesus' words drive us away from him. On the contrary, we must seek to understand these profound truths, as they are the key to our spiritual growth and relationship with Christ.

mots.sens: This term refers to human beings in general, but in the context of John, it specifically refers to Jesus as the Son of Man. This title emphasizes his incarnation and identification with humanity while affirming his divinity. The ascent of Jesus to heaven, mentioned in this verse, reinforces the idea of his preexistence and divine authority, reminding us that his ascension is an essential step in his redemptive work.

This verb means 'to ascend' or 'to rise.' It evokes not only a physical movement to a higher place but also a spiritual elevation. In the context of this verse, it highlights the ascension of Jesus to heaven, marking the end of his earthly ministry and the beginning of his heavenly reign. This has significant theological implications, as it confirms Christ's sovereignty and his role as intercessor before the Father.

This term means 'before' or 'previously.' It indicates a return to a prior state, emphasizing that Jesus existed before his incarnation. This reinforces the doctrine of the preexistence of Christ, affirming that he is not merely a man, but the Son of God who left heavenly glory to become man. Spiritually, this reminds us that our salvation is anchored in the eternal reality of Christ.

62.epoque: The historical context of this passage is set in the first century, during Jesus' ministry in Galilee, where he taught and performed miracles before a growing crowd. It was a time of great messianic expectation among the Jewish people, who hoped for a political and spiritual savior.
62.passage: This verse is found in chapter 6 of the Gospel of John, where Jesus teaches about the bread of life. After multiplying the loaves and fish, he reveals profound truths about his divine identity and his role as the source of eternal life, provoking varied reactions among his disciples.
62.culture: In Jewish culture, the idea of ascension to heaven was linked to glorification and divine authority. The Jews awaited a Messiah who would establish an earthly kingdom, but Jesus redefines this expectation by showing that his kingdom is spiritual and eternal.
62.interpretation: The ascension of Jesus is a key moment that attests to his divinity and authority. By ascending to where he was before, he confirms his divine identity and redemptive mission. This also reminds us that our faith rests on a living and glorified Christ, who reigns in heaven.
62.commentaire: This verse invites us to reflect on the nature of our faith in Christ. By acknowledging that he ascended to heaven, we are called to live with the assurance that he is our intercessor and our king. This encourages us to seek the things above and to live as citizens of the kingdom of God, awaiting his glorious return.

mots.sens: The word 'pneuma' means 'spirit' and refers to the immaterial element of human beings, often associated with life and vitality. In the biblical context, it also represents the presence of God and his life-giving action in the lives of believers. This term emphasizes the importance of the spiritual dimension over the physical dimension, indicating that it is through the Spirit that one receives true life.

The term 'sarx' translates to 'flesh' and refers to human nature in its weakness and mortality. In Scripture, it is often used to evoke the desires and passions that oppose the Spirit. Here, it emphasizes that human efforts, without divine intervention, are futile and incapable of producing true life.

The word 'logos' means 'word' and refers not only to a verbal statement but also to divine reason and cosmic order. In the New Testament, it is often associated with Christ, the incarnate Word. In this verse, the words of Jesus are presented as having a life-giving nature, revealing their spiritual power and ability to transform the lives of those who receive them.

63.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, during Jesus' ministry in Israel, a period marked by Roman occupation and messianic expectations among the Jewish people.
63.passage: John 6 deals with Jesus' discourse on the bread of life, where he reveals his divine nature and the necessity of believing in him to obtain eternal life. This verse highlights the distinction between spiritual life and human efforts.
63.culture: In Jewish culture, the importance of spirit and word was central, with a strong belief in the power of God's word to create and give life. Jesus' teachings clash with traditional conceptions of law and rituals.
63.interpretation: This verse reminds us that true life does not come from our physical efforts or human nature, but from the Spirit of God and the words of Christ. It invites us to seek spiritual life rather than rely on our own abilities.
63.commentaire: In our daily lives, we are often tempted to rely on our own strengths and skills. This verse calls us to recognize our dependence on the Spirit to be truly revitalized. By meditating on the words of Jesus, we can find the life and transformation we seek, encouraging us to nourish our spirit rather than our flesh.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to believe' or 'to have faith'. In the context of John 6:64, it refers to a deep and personal trust in Jesus as the Messiah. The root of this word evokes the idea of relying on someone or something, thus highlighting the importance of authentic faith in the relationship with Christ. Spiritually, it reminds us that faith is not merely an intellectual assent, but a commitment of the heart.

This term means 'to know' or 'to understand'. In this verse, it emphasizes Jesus' omniscient knowledge, which encompasses not only believers but also those who doubt or reject faith. This word highlights the depth of the relationship between Jesus and his disciples, where he intimately knows their hearts and intentions, which has theological implications regarding God's sovereignty and the nature of faith.

This verb means 'to deliver' or 'to betray'. In the context of John 6:64, it refers to the betrayal of Judas Iscariot, who will deliver Jesus to the authorities. This word evokes themes of loyalty and betrayal, underscoring the tragic consequences of a lack of faith and disobedience, while also highlighting God's sovereign plan for salvation.

64.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, during Jesus' ministry in Israel, a period marked by messianic expectations and religious tensions between the Jews and the Roman authorities.
64.passage: John 6 deals with Jesus' teaching on the bread of life, where he reveals his divine nature and role as Savior. This verse emphasizes the fact that even among his disciples, some did not truly believe in him, which sets the stage for the tragic events to come.
64.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, faith and belief were central elements of religious identity. Expectations regarding the Messiah were high, and the betrayal of a disciple would have been particularly shocking and significant in this context.
64.interpretation: This verse reminds us that authentic faith is essential for following Jesus. It highlights Christ's perfect knowledge, who knows who follows him sincerely and who betrays him, thus underscoring the importance of spiritual integrity in our relationship with him.
64.commentaire: John 6:64 challenges us regarding our own faith and commitment to Christ. It is crucial to examine our hearts and ensure that our belief in Jesus is authentic and deep. By recognizing Jesus' perfect knowledge, we are called to live a faith that manifests through actions and consistent faithfulness, even in the face of doubts and challenges.

mots.sens: This term means 'gift' or 'present'. It evokes the idea of a favor granted without expectation of return, highlighting divine grace. In the context of John 6:65, it underscores that access to Christ is a gift from the Father, thus emphasizing the divine initiative in salvation and the importance of grace in the relationship between God and man.

This verb means 'to come' or 'to arrive'. It implies a movement toward a place or a person. In this verse, it emphasizes that coming to Jesus is not merely a physical act, but a spiritual act that requires a divine invitation, reinforcing the idea that salvation is a work of God and not the result of our efforts.

This word means 'father'. In the biblical context, it represents not only a familial relationship but also authority, protection, and love. Here, it highlights the relationship between the heavenly Father and those who are called to come to Christ, indicating that it is the Father who draws hearts to the Son.

This term means 'to give back' or 'to restore'. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes that the ability to come to Jesus is an act of divine grace, and that this gift cannot be earned or acquired by man. This highlights God's sovereignty in the process of salvation.

65.epoque: This passage was written in the first century, at a time when Judaism and the early Christian communities were seeking to understand the nature of divine revelation and salvation.
65.passage: John 6:65 is situated in a discourse where Jesus teaches about the bread of life, revealing his divine nature and mission. This verse concludes a series of teachings on the necessity of divine revelation to understand and accept Jesus.
65.culture: In Jesus' time, the notion of gift and grace was central in Jewish culture, where relationships with God were often perceived as based on obedience to the law. Jesus overturns this idea by asserting that access to him is a gift from the Father.
65.interpretation: This verse underscores God's sovereignty in the process of salvation. It reminds us that faith in Christ is not the result of a human choice, but a divine work that draws believers to him. This calls us to recognize our total dependence on God's grace.
65.commentaire: John 6:65 teaches us that coming to Christ is a privilege granted by the Father. It reminds us that our salvation rests entirely on grace and divine initiative. As believers, we must cultivate an attitude of gratitude for this precious gift and pray that others may also be drawn to him through the work of the Holy Spirit.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to go away' or 'to depart'. It evokes the idea of a voluntary departure, often in response to a change in situation or conviction. In the context of John 6:66, this departure symbolizes a rejection of Jesus' teaching, highlighting the difficulty some disciples had in accepting the depth of his spiritual revelation. Theologically, this underscores the reality of human choice in the face of divine calling.

This term designates a 'disciple' or 'student'. It implies a relationship of learning and following, where the disciple commits to learning from and imitating their master. In John 6:66, the fact that some 'disciples' withdraw shows that even those who were close to Jesus can choose not to follow him when his teachings become too difficult to accept. This reminds us that faith requires a constant commitment.

This verb means 'to come' or 'to arrive'. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the idea of presence and communion with Jesus. The fact that several disciples no longer 'come' to him after this moment indicates a rupture in the relationship, revealing the consequences of misunderstanding or rejecting his words. Spiritually, this challenges us regarding our own commitment to remain close to Christ despite challenges.

66.epoque: The historical context of this passage is set in the first century, in Palestine, where Jesus preaches and performs miracles, attracting many disciples while also provoking controversies among religious authorities.
66.passage: John 6 deals with Jesus' teaching on the 'bread of life', where he reveals himself as the source of eternal life. This verse, John 6:66, marks a turning point, illustrating the rejection of some disciples in the face of deep spiritual truths.
66.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, the idea of following a rabbi and accepting his teachings was central. The departure of these disciples shows the tensions between cultural expectations and the truths revealed by Jesus.
66.interpretation: This verse illustrates the reality of spiritual choice. The disciples who withdraw represent those who, faced with difficult teachings, prefer to abandon rather than engage in a deep faith. This reminds us that faith can be tested and that true discipleship requires a total acceptance of the truth of Christ.
66.commentaire: John 6:66 challenges us regarding our own commitment to Jesus. In the face of difficult truths, it is essential not to abandon our faith, but to seek understanding and growth. This passage encourages us to persevere in our walk with Christ, even when his teachings challenge us, for it is in this faithfulness that we find true life.

mots.sens: This verb means 'to depart' or 'to go away'. It evokes the idea of withdrawal, separation, or abandonment. In the context of this verse, it emphasizes the disciples' decision to either stay with Jesus or leave him, highlighting the notion of fidelity and commitment to the Master. Theologically, this recalls the call to follow Christ, even when the road becomes difficult.

This term translates to 'will' and implies a deep intention or desire. In the context of God's will, it refers to what is desired by God for humanity. Here, it questions the disciples about their own will in relation to that of Jesus, underscoring the importance of choosing to follow the divine path despite challenges.

This word means 'disciples' or 'learners'. It designates those who follow a master to learn from him. In this verse, it reminds us that the disciples are called to an active relationship with Jesus, where their commitment is tested, and it evokes the responsibility of every believer to remain faithful to the teaching of Christ.

67.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, in the context of Palestine under Roman rule, where Jesus' ministry generates both enthusiasm and controversy among the crowds and religious authorities.
67.passage: In John 6, Jesus teaches about the bread of life after performing the miracle of the multiplication of the loaves. The disciples, faced with difficult teachings, must decide whether to stay with him or leave.
67.culture: At that time, following a rabbi was a deep commitment, involving not only learning but also a shared life. The disciples had to weigh the cost of their commitment against social and religious expectations.
67.interpretation: Jesus' question to the twelve disciples highlights the challenge of authentic faith. It invites every believer to reflect on their own commitment to Christ, especially when teachings become difficult to accept.
67.commentaire: This verse reminds us that faith is not merely an intellectual assent, but a personal commitment. In the face of the challenges of the Christian life, we are called to remain faithful to our calling, even when the temptation to drift away is felt. Like the disciples, we must choose to follow Jesus, recognizing that his will is always for our good and spiritual growth.

mots.sens: The word 'logos' means 'word', 'speech', or 'reason'. In the context of John 6:68, it evokes not only spoken words but also a deep and living truth that gives meaning and direction to life. This term carries theological significance, as it refers to divine revelation and the authority of Christ, who is himself the incarnate 'Logos', the source of eternal life.

'Zoe' means 'life', but in a spiritual sense, it designates eternal life, the fullness of life that God offers. This term is distinct from 'bios', which refers to physical life. In this verse, Peter recognizes that Jesus holds the words that grant access to this eternal life, thus emphasizing the necessity of turning to Christ for true and lasting existence.

'Kyrios' means 'Lord' and denotes supreme authority. By addressing Jesus as 'Lord', Peter acknowledges Christ's divinity and his central role in salvation. This title implies a relationship of submission and devotion, affirming that Jesus is the one who guides and provides for the spiritual needs of his disciples.

68.epoque: The passage is set in the first century, in the context of Palestine under Roman occupation, where messianic expectations were high among the Jewish people, who hoped for a liberating Savior.
68.passage: John 6 deals with Jesus' teaching on the bread of life, where he reveals himself as the essential spiritual source. This chapter highlights the disciples' reaction to difficult teachings, and Peter's confession underscores the necessity of remaining attached to the truth revealed by Christ.
68.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, the words of rabbis were considered to have great authority, but here, Peter asserts that Jesus' words transcend those of traditional teachers, as they are linked to eternal life.
68.interpretation: Peter's response is a declaration of faith and dependence on Jesus. It emphasizes that, in the face of uncertainties and challenges, there is no other source of truth and life than that which Jesus offers, calling for total trust in him.
68.commentaire: This verse reminds us that, in moments of doubt or crisis, our response should be to turn to Jesus, who holds the words of eternal life. As believers, we are called to affirm our faith in him and seek his truth to guide our lives. This encourages us to deepen our relationship with Christ, for it is in him that we find the fullness of life.

mots.sens: The term 'Christos' means 'anointed' and is the Greek translation of the Hebrew word 'Messiah'. In the biblical context, it designates one who has been chosen and consecrated by God to fulfill a divine mission, particularly that of saving his people. By affirming that Jesus is the Christ, the disciples recognize not only his saving role but also his divine authority and unique identity as the Son of God.

The word 'hagios' means 'sacred' or 'holy', and it is used to designate what is set apart for God. In this verse, it emphasizes the divine and perfect nature of Jesus, who is both fully human and fully divine. This recognition of Jesus as 'the Holy One of God' implies a deep understanding of his purity, holiness, and unique role in the redemption of humanity.

The verb 'pisteuō' means 'to believe' or 'to have faith'. In the New Testament, it expresses a deep and personal trust in God and in Jesus Christ. The faith of the disciples, affirmed in this verse, is not merely intellectual but also relational, involving a total commitment to the person of Jesus as Savior and Lord.

The verb 'ginōskō' means 'to know' in a deep and intimate sense. It goes beyond mere intellectual knowledge to include a personal and relational experience. In this verse, it underscores that the faith of the disciples is based on a personal knowledge of Jesus, which has led them to recognize his divine identity and saving work.

69.epoque: This passage is set in the first century, during the earthly ministry of Jesus, a period marked by Roman occupation and messianic expectations among the Jewish people.
69.passage: John 6 deals with Jesus' teaching on the bread of life, where he reveals himself as the essential spiritual source for eternal life. This verse follows the disciples' reaction to Jesus' difficult teaching, highlighting their commitment to him.
69.culture: In the Jewish culture of the time, the idea of the Messiah was deeply rooted, with expectations of deliverance and restoration. Recognizing Jesus as the Christ and the Holy One of God was a bold act of faith in opposition to established religious authorities.
69.interpretation: This verse illustrates the disciples' confession of faith, recognizing Jesus not only as a teacher but as the promised Messiah and the Holy One of God. It underscores the importance of faith and personal knowledge of Jesus for entering into a true relationship with him.
69.commentaire: John 6:69 reminds us that faith in Jesus rests on a personal knowledge and experience of his holiness and redemptive work. As believers, we are called to deepen our understanding of who Jesus is and affirm our faith in him as the Christ, the Holy One of God. This recognition should transform our daily lives and our relationship with him.

mots.sens: This term refers to a spirit or a demon, often associated with malevolent influence. In the context of this verse, it highlights betrayal and duplicity, referencing Judas Iscariot, who, although one of the twelve disciples chosen by Jesus, is described as being under the influence of an evil spirit. This underscores the spiritual struggle between good and evil and reminds believers of the necessity to remain vigilant against temptations.

This verb means 'to choose' or 'to select', and in this context, it emphasizes the divine action of Jesus in choosing His disciples. It implies intention and a divine plan, revealing that even among those who are chosen, there may be hearts that turn away from God. This reminds us that God's choice does not guarantee the faithfulness of each individual, and our response to this call is crucial.

Meaning 'sent one', this term describes the role of the disciples as messengers of the Gospel. In this verse, it emphasizes the responsibility that falls on those who are chosen to serve and testify to the truth of Christ. It evokes the idea that the call to serve God is serious and requires constant integrity and faithfulness, as even those who are called can fail.

70.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, within the context of Jesus' ministry in Palestine, a period marked by religious and political tensions between the Jews and the Romans.
70.passage: John 6 deals with Jesus' teaching on the bread of life, where He reveals His divine nature and salvific role. This verse highlights the reality of betrayal even among those who are close to Him.
70.culture: At that time, the choice of disciples was a significant act, involving a relationship of learning and mentorship. The notion of betrayal was particularly shocking in a context where loyalty was valued.
70.interpretation: By acknowledging that He has chosen His disciples, Jesus underscores the seriousness of Judas' betrayal. This teaches us that even among those called to follow Christ, there may be hearts that turn away, highlighting the importance of spiritual vigilance.
70.commentaire: This verse reminds us of the reality of betrayal in our walk with God. As believers, we must be aware that our commitment to Christ requires constant faithfulness. It is essential to cultivate our relationship with Him in order to remain steadfast in our calling and avoid the pitfalls of duplicity.

mots.sens: The name 'Ioudas' (Judas) means 'praised' or 'one who praises'. In the biblical context, Judas Iscariot is often associated with betrayal and disloyalty, which stands in stark contrast to his name. The root of the name evokes an identity that could have been that of a faithful servant, but which is tragically perverted. Theologically, this reminds us that even those who are close to Jesus can choose to turn away from the truth.

This verb means 'to deliver' or 'to hand over'. In the New Testament, it is often used to refer to the handing over of Jesus to the authorities, symbolizing betrayal. The spiritual significance of this word underscores the gravity of Judas' choice, who, by delivering Jesus, not only betrayed his Master but also participated in the fulfillment of the divine plan of redemption. This challenges us regarding the nature of our choices and their impact on our relationship with God.

The term 'δώδεκα' means 'twelve', and in the context of the disciples, it represents fullness and divine authority. The twelve disciples are the foundations of the Church, and their number symbolizes unity and mission. The fact that Judas, one of the twelve, is the one who betrays Jesus highlights the reality of sin even among those called to be spiritual leaders. This reminds us that proximity to Christ does not guarantee faithfulness.

71.epoque: This passage is set in the 1st century, during Jesus' ministry in Israel, a period marked by religious and political tensions between the Jews and the Roman occupiers.
71.passage: In John 6, Jesus teaches about the bread of life, and this verse is part of a broader discourse where He reveals the nature of His ministry and the necessity of faith. The mention of Judas in this context underscores the seriousness of betrayal even among those close to Jesus.
71.culture: At that time, betrayal was considered one of the worst acts of infidelity, especially in a context where loyalty and honor were paramount. Judas, as a disciple, held a privileged position, and his betrayal would have been perceived as an affront not only to Jesus but also to the community of disciples.
71.interpretation: This verse reminds us that even those who are called and chosen can make destructive choices. The mention of Judas as 'one of the twelve' highlights the tragedy of his decision, which led to the crucifixion of Jesus, but also to the fulfillment of God's salvation plan.
71.commentaire: This passage invites us to reflect on our own faithfulness to Christ. Like Judas, we can be close to Jesus and yet turn away from Him through our choices. This calls us to constant vigilance and a deep dependence on the Holy Spirit to remain faithful in our walk with the Lord.
